result: The ROOT & SHOOT Research Coordination Network was established in 2021 through NSF funding, involving seven plant science professional societies with the goal of advancing diversity, equity, and inclusion, including a commitment to safer and more inclusive conferences.
evaluation: Claims C8-C13 provide factual documentation of the project's establishment, funding, participating organizations, and stated objectives. These are verifiable administrative facts supported by citations and Table 1 data, representing the foundational context of the work.

result: ROOT & SHOOT established a working group approach to tackle inclusivity issues, deliberately recruiting diverse volunteers through an open call process that prioritized early-career researchers and used free-form questions rather than traditional credentials. The Inclusive Conference Working Group consisted of 24 members (17 with prior conference organizing experience) divided into five subgroups, with participants committing 6 hours/month for six months and receiving stipends.
evaluation: Claims C29-C73 describe the working group methodology with specific, verifiable details about recruitment, structure, time commitments, and participant characteristics. The approach is well-documented with citations supporting the consensus-trust decision-making model (C33, C34). Figure 1 provides demographic data supporting the diversity claims.

result: The Working Group developed comprehensive recommendations for inclusive conferences including community agreements, reporting structures, site selection guidance, accessibility measures, and equitable programming strategies. However, the aspirational community agreement was not adopted by conferences as described, due to perceived redundancy with existing Codes of Conduct and enforceability concerns, though one conference plans to incorporate some language.
evaluation: Claims C74-C82 document both the development of recommendations and their limited implementation. The acknowledgment of non-adoption (C81) and reasons provided (redundancy, enforceability concerns) demonstrates honest reporting of outcomes. Table 2 provides implementation tracking data across conferences.

result: ROOT & SHOOT partnered with ADVANCEGeo to provide free bystander intervention training workshops, hosting seven sessions since 2023 with an average of 53 participants per session. The three-hour training format included two hours of instruction and one hour of practice. Organizations varied in their approach (some requiring attendance for session chairs, others incentivizing with badge stickers), and anecdotal feedback indicated increased confidence in intervening, though no formal post-training evaluations were conducted.
evaluation: Claims C127-C145 provide specific quantitative data (7 sessions, 53 average participants, 3-hour format) but rely entirely on anecdotal feedback (C143, C144) rather than systematic evaluation. The lack of formal assessment (C143) and reliance on informal reports undermines confidence in the claimed effectiveness. The variation in organizational adoption suggests mixed commitment.

result: ROOT & SHOOT funded professional ombudsperson services at five conferences over two years (costing $8,000-$15,000 per conference). The service was utilized at least once at each conference, addressing issues including harassment, bias, and accessibility concerns. Limited evaluation data from two conferences showed 66% awareness, 63% understanding of purpose, and 47% finding it important, with 35% rating it high value at another conference. Cost remains a significant barrier to sustainability.
evaluation: Claims C146-C171 document implementation with specific cost data and utilization metrics. However, evaluation is severely limited (C159: only two conferences provided data) and sample sizes are small (n=165-191). The mixed reception (C164: 47% important, 39% neutral, 13% disagreed) and limited data collection undermine strong conclusions about effectiveness. The acknowledgment of cost barriers (C166) and limited sustainability (C167) is appropriate.

result: ROOT & SHOOT explored restorative justice approaches to address harm at conferences, initiating community conversations in early 2024 and drafting an initial accountability process guide. However, the majority of community members have not participated in this process, and the authors acknowledge the community may not be ready to fully engage in this discussion.
evaluation: Claims C172-C186 describe exploratory work on restorative justice with appropriate acknowledgment of limited community engagement (C185). The work remains in draft form (C183, C184) with no implementation or evaluation data. The honest assessment of community readiness (C186) is appropriate, but this represents aspirational rather than demonstrated work.

result: Engaging diverse stakeholders from different backgrounds, societies, and career stages increased members' sense of belonging (especially early-career scientists), raised previously unconsidered issues (dietary restrictions, safety concerns, religious conflicts), and increased organizational commitment to implementing recommendations.
evaluation: Claims C187-C191 make strong assertions about impact (increased belonging, raised awareness, increased commitment) but provide no empirical evidence, systematic evaluation, or quantitative data. These are entirely inferential claims (all marked as INFERENCE in evidence_type) without supporting measurements. The claimed outcomes require formal assessment to be credible.

result: The Working Group faced challenges including coordinating 30 people across time zones, completing work slower than anticipated, and balancing flexibility with structure. Future recommendations include smaller core groups with advisory networks, more structured frameworks with clearer timelines, and iterative feedback from multiple conference rounds.
evaluation: Claims C192-C197 provide honest reflection on operational challenges with specific details (30 people, time zones, timeline delays). The recommendations for future work (C193, C195, C197) are appropriately framed as speculative suggestions rather than validated solutions. This represents valuable lessons learned.

result: Implementation challenges arose primarily from cost barriers, with societies agreeing with recommendations in principle but facing budgetary constraints. Organizations vary in size and funding models, and some recommendations (ASL interpreters, ombudsperson services) incur significant costs ($8,000-$15,000). Legal requirements vary internationally, and ROOT & SHOOT aimed to demonstrate value to encourage sustained implementation beyond the funding period.
evaluation: Claims C198-C208 provide specific cost data and honest assessment of implementation barriers. The acknowledgment that organizations agreed in principle but faced practical barriers (C198) is appropriately documented. The specific example of ASL interpreter costs and requirements (C202-C204) provides concrete illustration. Future sustainability concerns (C207, C208) are appropriately framed as speculative.

result: One society declined the ombudsperson service due to perceived duplication and liability concerns, while two conferences that used the service elected to continue funding it in future years.
evaluation: Claims C209-C211 document variable adoption with specific examples of both rejection and continuation. This demonstrates honest reporting of mixed outcomes and provides insight into organizational decision-making factors.

result: Assessment of outcomes was challenging due to different societies using different evaluation tools, with requests to include specific questions generally unsuccessful. Where data were gathered, small numbers of individuals engaged with interventions, raising questions about how to interpret impact and prioritize interventions affecting small numbers of people.
evaluation: Claims C212-C216 honestly acknowledge evaluation limitations and raise important methodological questions about assessing interventions with limited uptake. The acknowledgment of unsuccessful data collection efforts (C213) and interpretive challenges (C215, C216) demonstrates appropriate scientific humility about drawing conclusions from limited data.

result: Unwelcoming climate and culture at scientific conferences is an obstacle to retaining scientists with marginalized identities, with inequities stemming from white supremacy, cis-hetero-normativity, inaccessible facilities, unwelcoming environments, and biases manifesting in both explicit and implicit practices. Hostile cultures persist in research and academic settings, with conferences being particularly risky places.
evaluation: Claims C1-C14 establish the problem context with appropriate citations (Jack-Scott 2023, Berhe et al. 2022). While C1 lacks direct citation in that sentence, the general claim is well-established in DEI literature and supported by the cited work in C4 and C14. These provide appropriate motivation for the work.

result: Despite bleak short-term prospects for federal funding of inclusion work, most recommendations can be implemented without significant cost (community agreements, accessibility information, food labeling, family-friendly spaces, gender-neutral bathrooms, diverse programming). Community volunteers can accomplish many tasks, efforts can be carried out discreetly if necessary, and those who benefit will be aware of the efforts made.
evaluation: Claims C218-C223 make important practical recommendations but mix factual statements about low-cost options (C219) with speculative claims about volunteer capacity (C221), discretion (C222), and awareness (C223). The assertion that beneficiaries will be aware (C223) lacks empirical support. The political context statement (C218) is appropriately framed as speculation but may date quickly.

result: The Working Group developed site selection guidance recommending transparency in decision-making, reasonable costs with subsidies, accessible venues with accommodation information, and safe locations (reproductive services available, LGBTQ+ protections, visa accessibility). Several conferences adopted safety-related recommendations.
evaluation: Claims C95-C102 document specific recommendations with supporting materials (Supplementary file 3) and implementation tracking (Table 2). The recommendations are concrete and actionable, with documented partial adoption (C102) showing real-world application.

result: The Working Group developed extensive accessibility recommendations covering five aspects (economic, physical, audio/visual, family, wellness), comprising the largest section of the guide. Recommendations include closed captioning, all-gender bathrooms, childcare, lactation rooms, quiet/scent-free spaces (given 20%+ neurodiversity prevalence), and clearly labeled food with allergen information. Some accessibility options may conflict, requiring long-term balancing.
evaluation: Claims C103-C113 provide comprehensive accessibility recommendations with supporting documentation (Supplementary file 4). The 20% neurodiversity statistic (C110) is stated as fact but lacks citation—this should be verified. The acknowledgment of potential conflicts between accessibility options (C105) shows sophisticated understanding of implementation challenges.

result: The Working Group developed recommendations for diverse speaker selection including inviting first authors rather than senior authors, including historically underrepresented topics (Indigenous knowledge, science policy, history, education), ensuring diverse program committees (which studies show generate diverse speaker lists), using correct pronouns and name pronunciation, and tracking diversity data year-over-year for accountability.
evaluation: Claims C114-C124 provide concrete, actionable recommendations with appropriate citation support for the claim about diverse committees generating diverse speakers (C119, C120: Segarra et al. 2020). The recommendations are specific and measurable, with appropriate emphasis on transparency and accountability (C123, C124).
